content: Flat feet, also known as pes planus or fallen arches, is a condition where the arch of the foot collapses, causing the entire sole of the foot to come into full or nearly full contact with the ground. In some individuals, estimated to be 20-30% of the population, the arch never develops in one or both feet. It is important to note that having flat feet does not reduce foot speed. Flat Feet in Children Flat feet are common and normal in infants due to the presence of baby fat, which obscures the developing arch, and because the arch has not yet fully formed. The human foot arch develops during infancy and early childhood as part of normal growth of muscles, tendons, ligaments, and bones. Activities such as foot gymnastics and walking barefoot on varied terrain can promote the formation of arches during childhood, with most children developing a visible arch by the age of four to six years. Parents or caregivers should monitor children for flat feet, as young children are unlikely to recognize or report the condition themselves. Visual inspection is helpful, but parents should also observe for unusual walking patterns, such as walking on the outer edges of the feet, limping during long walks, or complaints of foot pain, which some children describe as feeling like a nail piercing the foot. Complaints of calf muscle pain or other discomfort around the foot area may also indicate flat feet. Recent medical research suggests that arch support inserts and certain heel cups, when placed in a growing child’s shoes, can aid in the proper development of the longitudinal arch by maintaining the foot in a neutral position during growth. However, walking barefoot, especially on uneven surfaces like sand, is generally beneficial for most children, except for those with extremely flat feet or related conditions such as plantar fasciitis. A study conducted in India found that children who grew up walking barefoot had stronger and higher arches as a group, and flat feet were less common among children who wore sandals or slippers compared to those who wore closed-toe shoes. Flat Feet in Adults Flat feet can also develop in adulthood, a condition referred to as adult-acquired flatfoot. This can result from injury, illness, prolonged or unusual stress on the foot, faulty biomechanics, or the natural aging process. Pregnant women may experience temporary flat feet due to increased elasticity (elastin) during pregnancy. However, if flat feet develop in adulthood, they are generally permanent. If an adult or youth appears flat-footed while standing in a full weight-bearing position but shows an arch when standing on tiptoes or dorsiflexing the foot, this is termed flexible flatfoot. While muscular training of the feet can be beneficial, it typically does not increase arch height in adults because the muscles in the human foot are too short for exercise to make a significant difference. However, as long as the foot is still growing, there remains a possibility of creating a lasting arch. Diagnosis and Treatment A podiatrist can easily diagnose flat feet during an office visit. A simple home test, known as the wet foot test, involves wetting the feet and standing on a surface like cement or heavy paper. If the footprint shows no dry area where the arch should be, it is a strong indication of flat feet. Most cases of flexible flat feet are asymptomatic and not painful, requiring no cause for concern. However, rigid flatfoot, where the sole remains flat even when not weight-bearing, can be a cause for concern. Other conditions related to flat feet, such as tarsal coalition (abnormal joining of two or more bones in the midfoot or hindfoot) or accessory navicular (an extra bone on the side of the foot), should be treated promptly, ideally during early adolescence before the bone structure becomes permanently set. These conditions can be confirmed through X-rays. Treatment for flat feet may be necessary if there is associated pain in the foot or lower leg, or if the condition affects the knees or back. Treatment options include the use of arch supports or orthotics, foot exercises, or other interventions recommended by a podiatrist or physician. Surgery, while a last resort, can provide lasting relief and even create an arch where none previously existed, though it is typically expensive. Research on Arch Height and Stress Fractures Several studies have explored the relationship between arch height and stress fractures. One study of 287 Israeli Defense Force recruits found that individuals with high arches experienced nearly four times as many stress fractures as those with the lowest arches. However, a later study of 449 U.S. naval special warfare trainees found no significant difference in stress fracture incidence among individuals with varying arch heights, and another study yielded inconclusive results.
